In engineering, integrity and honesty are limited resources you introduce only once in your career . If you do not know something, you must say so and find out—misrepresenting knowledge erodes the trust that is essential when your designs affect people's lives.

This principle, learned from foundational Hydro engineer Elemar McKay, sits at the foundation of engineering ethics. The core idea is simple but unforgiving: once your reputation for honesty is damaged, it cannot be fully restored . In a profession where decisions directly impact human safety, that loss of trust becomes catastrophic.

The distinction matters. Other professions can often recover from lapses in credibility or recover from limited misjudgments. Engineering is different. As Glenn Powell explains in the episode , when engineers design systems affecting people's lives—whether it's a pump in a critical infrastructure application or a pressure relief valve in a hazardous environment—perfect honesty is not a luxury, it is a necessity.

The practical implication is direct: admit uncertainty rather than guess . If you lack knowledge in a specific area, the ethical response is not to bluff your way through or present partial understanding as complete expertise. Instead, acknowledge the gap explicitly and commit to finding the answer. This builds credibility rather than eroding it.

This principle also reflects a deeper truth about engineering culture. Knowledge builds on previous work—if the foundation is dishonest, everything built above it becomes unstable. A junior engineer who hides a knowledge gap may pass that problem to colleagues downstream, creating hidden risks. A senior engineer who misrepresents expertise can lead entire teams off course.

The logic extends to team dynamics. In discussions on how Hydro approaches complex projects , this ethic shows up constantly: engineers who will openly say "I don't know, but let me research this" are trusted far more than those who speculate or overstate their capabilities. Why this matters more in engineering than elsewhere

Engineering is one of the few professions where a dishonest decision doesn't just affect a business outcome—it can directly harm people. A financial advisor who misrepresents market risk causes monetary loss. An engineer who misrepresents system capacity or material properties can cause injury or death. This asymmetry makes honesty non-negotiable, not aspirational.

It also means the standard for integrity is higher because the stakes are higher. You can often rebuild professional relationships in other fields through apologies, corrections, or time. In engineering, some decisions are irreversible—they're built into steel, concrete, or hydraulic systems that will operate for decades. Once you've cut corners or misled colleagues on a design, that mistake might be discovered only when the system fails in the field.

For anyone building a career in technical fields, this principle from Elemar McKay is worth internalizing early. The full conversation with Glenn Powell explores how this ethic plays out across Hydro's approach to reliability, testing, and innovation—showing that engineering excellence and professional integrity are not separate virtues, they are the same thing.

Commercial real estate careers split between two economic models: the time-and-effort economy, where income depends on showing up and working your hours, and the results economy, where income is entirely tied to what you produce, regardless of hours spent. The industry has traditionally been results-focused, but it is shifting to include more stable time-and-effort roles like property managers and salary-based positions blending base pay with commission—and choosing the right model for your temperament is essential to long-term career satisfaction.
The two models and how they shape your career

In the time-and-effort economy, you are paid for your presence and labor —salary, hourly wages, or benefits tied to consistent work. This model appeals to people who value predictability, security, and a stable paycheck. You know exactly what you will earn each month, and there is no risk of income collapse if you hit a temporary market downturn or a slow sales cycle.

The results economy operates on the opposite principle: your income depends entirely on outcomes you produce —commissions on deals closed, profits from investments, or revenue from your client base. There is no safety net; if you don't sell, you don't earn. But there is also no ceiling: your income is limited only by your ability to generate results.

Historically, commercial real estate has been built on the results economy . Brokers earn commissions, investors profit from deal performance, developers reap returns from projects. But as discussed in the Commercially Speaking Podcast episode , the industry is evolving. Property managers, asset managers, and increasingly, brokerage firms are offering salary-based and hybrid compensation packages that blend base pay with performance incentives, creating a middle ground for professionals who don't want pure commission risk.
Matching the model to your temperament and life stage

Not everyone thrives under the same system. Results-based roles demand tolerance for uncertainty and the ability to self-motivate without a guaranteed paycheck . They suit people who are competitive, driven by control, and willing to bet on their own productivity. They also require either capital reserves or the freedom to survive lean periods—a significant barrier for early-career professionals or anyone with dependents.

Time-and-effort roles attract people who prioritize security and prefer a predictable income stream . They work well for those managing family obligations, building an emergency fund, or simply wanting to separate their livelihood from the stress of variable earnings. As explained in this podcast , some professionals need this stability to function at their best; others feel constrained by it.

The critical insight is that one model is not superior to the other. Career satisfaction hinges on alignment between your economic model and your personal values . Placing a high-energy, self-directed person in a salaried role can lead to frustration and underperformance. Similarly, forcing a security-minded professional into pure commission work creates constant anxiety. Understanding which economy you belong in is a prerequisite for long-term success in commercial real estate.

Billionaire investors start by asking one question: how do I avoid losing money? Capital preservation comes before chasing returns. Warren Buffett famously said the number one rule of investing is don't lose money, and the number two rule is don't forget rule number one. A volatile portfolio with high returns actually leaves you with less money at the end than a steady, boring one—because losses interrupt compounding.
Why compounding breaks when losses hit

The difference between a billionaire investor and an everyday investor isn't about ambition or risk tolerance—it's about understanding what stops growth dead. When you lose money, you don't just lose the capital itself. You lose all the future compounding that money would have generated. If you're down 20%, you need a 25% return just to break even. Down 50%? You need a 100% gain to recover.

This is why portfolio volatility becomes a silent wealth killer. Two portfolios might show the same average return on paper, but the one that swings wildly—booming one year, crashing the next—will end with less total wealth. The math is ruthless: steady compounding at 8% beats erratic swings between +20% and -10% even when the arithmetic average looks identical.
The risk-first framework that separates the winners

As Bob Frazier explains in the episode , this mentality shows up in how billionaires structure their portfolios. They don't ask "How much can I make?" first. They ask "Where does this break? What's the downside? What happens if everything goes wrong?" Only after stress-testing the worst case do they build the upside on top.

This is the opposite of how most everyday investors think. The common approach is to find a promising opportunity, hope it works out, and cross fingers. Billionaires reverse the order entirely. They design portfolios that can survive a downturn, then stack gains on top of a stable foundation. The result: less volatility, more compound wealth, and peace of mind.
"The first thing you want to focus on is not losing money. Warren Buffett said the number one rule of investing is don't lose money. The number two rule is don't forget rule number one."

The problem runs deeper than sentiment. When everyone who believes a stock will rise has already purchased it, the buying pressure disappears. Valuation as a Timing Signal

Historical valuation metrics do not predict short-term price movements, but over longer periods they constrain returns mathematically. When the price-to-earnings ratio sits at historically extreme levels, future returns compress simply because the denominator—future earnings growth—must be extraordinary to justify current prices, and extraordinary growth rarely materializes.

This is not opinion; it is arithmetic. If you buy a stock at 40 times earnings and earnings grow modestly, the stock cannot deliver the same returns it delivered when bought at 20 times earnings. The math is fixed. For this reason, Frazier discusses how understanding valuation cycles helps investors avoid the trap of chasing recent winners , which often represent the end of a cycle rather than the beginning.

Reg D 506C removes the ban on general advertising for private investment deals, allowing issuers to publicly market offerings to accredited investors —those meeting specific SEC wealth or income thresholds. Only accredited investors can participate, making it a pathway for alternative investments like private credit to reach a broader audience while maintaining regulatory compliance.
The accredited investor threshold that unlocks market access

The SEC defines accredited investors by clear, measurable criteria: $1 million in net worth excluding your primary home , or $200,000 in annual income (individually) or $300,000 as a combined household income. These thresholds determine who legally qualifies to invest in Reg D 506C offerings.

As Bob Frazier explains in the episode , this regulatory framework is what allows firms like Aspen Funds to market alternative investments directly rather than relying on private networks and referrals alone. The certification removes friction from capital raising by allowing deals to be advertised openly to a defined, qualified pool of investors.
Why marketing permission changes the deal-raising game

Traditional private offerings under other Reg D exemptions required no public advertising whatsoever —all investors had to come through existing relationships. Reg D 506C flips this entirely, permitting issuers to actively promote their deals while the accreditation requirement acts as the legal gatekeeper.

This matters because, as discussed in this conversation on alternative investment strategy , the bottleneck in raising capital is rarely the deals themselves—it's finding investors who have both capital and sophistication. Reg D 506C solves for reach without sacrificing safety, letting firms scale their capital base faster than cold pitching ever could.

He found re-performing notes, a category most investors overlook . The borrower had already demonstrated willingness and ability to pay again—the hardest part of credit assessment was already complete.

Vacancy control—the mechanism preventing rent resets when tenants leave an apartment—is the core policy that has destabilized the rent-stabilized market since the 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act. By capping increases to just 3.47% through Individual Apartment Improvements , the law sits far below the $1,300 average annual operating costs, making it economically unsustainable for landlords and removing an estimated minimum of 50,000 apartments from the housing supply.
How Vacancy Control Works Against Market Supply

Under vacancy control, when a tenant vacates a rent-stabilized apartment, the incoming tenant begins their lease at essentially the same rent as the previous occupant—with only a maximum Individual Apartment Improvement (IAI) increase of 3.47% allowed. This is dramatically different from vacancy bonus systems used in other jurisdictions, which allow landlords to reset rent closer to market rates when units turn over.

As Kenny Burgos explains in this episode of Coffee & Cap Rates , the math is straightforward: operating costs routinely exceed 1,300 dollars annually per unit in rent-stabilized buildings, yet the allowable rent increase caps out at 3.47%. Landlords cannot recover their investment in maintenance, repairs, utilities, or property taxes—let alone generate returns needed for capital improvements or refinancing.

The result has been a flight from the market. Buildings that had any liquidity or financing flexibility have been sold off, converted, or abandoned. Properties that once had market value have plummeted in price— selling for as little as $50,000 per unit in the Bronx , prices not seen since the 1980s.
The Scale of Housing Supply Loss

The policy impact is quantifiable and severe. An estimated minimum of 50,000 rent-stabilized apartments have been removed from the market since the 2019 law took effect. These units are no longer available to tenants—they've been converted, deconverted, or simply held off the market as owners wait for regulatory change or exit opportunities.

When Burgos discusses the state of vacancy control in the full podcast episode , he points to a deeper paradox: a policy designed to protect tenants has actually reduced the supply available to the next generation of renters. Over 80% of the 1 million rent-stabilized units citywide are pre-1974 housing stock—aging buildings that increasingly cannot afford basic maintenance under the current regulatory framework.

"A vacancy reset does not increase rent on any single in-place tenant today, it doesn't cost the city or state government a dollar, and it brings housing supply on the market, softening free market rents."

Broader Market Consequences

The damage extends far beyond individual landlords. Building valuations have fallen by 50% to 60% in rent-stabilized properties since the law's implementation. This erodes the collateral base for refinancing, blocks reinvestment in neighborhoods, and eliminates capital that might otherwise flow into new construction or preservation.

Burgos explores a related phenomenon in the episode : the role of major institutional bankruptcies like Flagstar's $451 million transaction, which dominated rent-stabilized deal flow in early 2026 and signaled the depth of distress in the sector. When the largest transactions in a market are bankruptcy sales, it tells you the market itself is in crisis.

For investors and policymakers alike, the lesson is clear: rental supply constraints are not solved by price controls —they are deepened by them. The 2019 law was intended to protect existing tenants, and it does. But the vacancy control mechanism has inadvertently become the primary driver reducing the total stock available to New Yorkers seeking housing.

Four separate financial shocks have converged on rent-stabilized buildings simultaneously: the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (HSTPA) capped rent growth on vacant units; COVID-19 created persistent 10–20% collection losses and economic vacancy that persists into 2026; interest rates spiked in 2022, multiplying debt burdens; and insurance premiums surged dramatically. Together, these forces have squeezed owner finances so tightly that building violations and Alternative Enforcement Program violations have risen sharply—like a hockey stick since 2022—because owners can no longer afford basic maintenance and repairs.
The cascade: Four shocks hitting simultaneously

HSTPA was passed in 2019 specifically to restrict rent growth on vacant apartments, preventing what the law called "vacancy bonuses." In principle, this protected tenancy rights; in practice, it removed a critical revenue lever for building owners. When combined with the pandemic's economic shock starting in 2020 , the effect became devastating.

COVID-19 didn't just create temporary vacancy—it fractured the collection model. Landlords faced 10–15–20% collection problems across their portfolios, and those problems have never fully healed. Tenant nonpayment and economic vacancy, when layered on top of a law that forbids raising rents on empty units, meant cash flow simply vanished.

Then in 2022, the Federal Reserve's aggressive rate hikes hit. For owners already carrying debt on aging buildings , the jump in interest rates translated directly to higher debt service and squeezed reserves even further. A building that was barely managing suddenly faced refinancing costs that made operations unsustainable.

Finally, insurance premiums exploded. Labor costs, litigation risk, and property damage claims all spiked, and rent-stabilized buildings—many built before 1974, with aging systems and higher maintenance risk—saw the largest percentage increases. As Kenny Burgos explains in the episode , owners reached the breaking point.
The physical consequence: Deferred maintenance becomes policy

When owners run out of money, they don't stop operations immediately—they defer maintenance. They skip elevator servicing, delay roof repairs, postpone plumbing fixes, reduce staffing. This is not neglect born of greed; it is financial constraint forcing a choice.

The result is visible in violation data: building violations and Alternative Enforcement Program (AEP) violations have risen sharply since 2022 , almost like a hockey stick. These are not violations born of negligence but of owners who genuinely cannot afford to fix problems at the pace the city expects.

Over 80% of the rent-stabilized stock consists of pre-1974 buildings—older structures with outdated infrastructure and higher baseline maintenance needs. A younger building might survive a cash crunch with minor deferrals; a 50-year-old building cannot.

"A vacancy reset does not increase rent on any single in-place tenant today, it doesn't cost the city or state government a dollar, and it brings housing supply on the market, softening free market rents."

Burgos's point highlights the policy dilemma: HSTPA was designed to protect tenants, but by removing the vacancy reset mechanism entirely , it has inadvertently destabilized the entire building stock. Owners lack the financial flexibility to weather multiple simultaneous shocks.

Over 80% of the 1 million rent-stabilized units in New York are pre-1974 buildings , permanently and involuntarily locked into rent stabilization by state law passed in 1974 as an emergency measure. Rent Stabilization Regulatory Framework: New York's rent stabilization system divides the market into two distinct cohorts based on construction date. Pre-1974 buildings are subject to mandatory, permanent rent stabilization under state law with no offsetting benefits. Post-1973 buildings are voluntary participants who accepted regulatory restrictions in return for specific tax abatements designed to offset operating constraints. The Pre-1974 Emergency Law That Still Governs the Majority

The state law that created permanent rent stabilization for pre-1974 buildings was passed as an emergency measure in 1974 , addressing a housing crisis at that moment. However, what was meant as temporary emergency policy became permanent and involuntary for owners of older buildings. Unlike post-1973 developments, pre-1974 building owners receive zero compensatory tax benefits.

This creates an asymmetry in the market: pre-1974 owners operate under full regulatory constraints while bearing the complete burden of full property taxes and all operating expenses —a $1,300 average annual operating cost per stabilized unit. The lack of any tax abatement or exemption means these buildings have no financial pathway to offset the restrictions on rent growth.
Post-1973 Buildings: A Voluntary Trade-Off

In stark contrast, post-1973 buildings—typically new developments—voluntarily chose to enter rent stabilization only when offered property tax exemptions like 421g or 485x programs . These builders and owners negotiated a deal: accept rent regulation in exchange for specific tax relief. This represented a conscious market choice, not a legal mandate.

Because post-1973 developments make up only a small fraction of the total rent-stabilized stock, the majority of affordable housing that developers contribute remains limited. The voluntary nature of post-1973 participation highlights the fundamental difference: pre-1974 owners had no choice and received nothing in return.

How aggregation masks building-level reality

The problem is structural. When their operational data is pooled with healthier segments, policymakers cannot see which buildings are genuinely failing and which are stable.
Why this distortion prevents solutions

The single-number approach forces officials to treat the entire rent-stabilized sector as a monolith, when in fact distinct financial cohorts need distinct interventions . A building averaging 1,300 dollars in annual operating costs per unit cannot be addressed with the same rent adjustment as a newer, more efficient property.

The aggregated metric also includes free market and mixed-regulated properties in its baseline, which further skews upward the apparent health of the stabilized stock. This distortion is discussed in detail in the podcast , where Burgos emphasizes that the board's methodology has become the largest obstacle to evidence-based policymaking.

A vacancy reset allows property owners to adjust rent when a unit becomes vacant, provided they invest in bringing the apartment to current housing code standards—including lead removal, asbestos remediation, and infrastructure upgrades. The next tenant receives full rent-stabilization protections, while no current in-place tenant sees their rent increase. The mechanism generates no government cost while improving building valuations and adding housing supply to the market.

The vacancy reset addresses a structural contradiction in New York's rent-stabilization system. Property owners face mounting operating costs— averaging $1,300 per apartment annually —while prohibited from raising rents on existing tenants or recouping investment through capital improvements at the pace required to maintain buildings. This creates a cascading problem: buildings deteriorate, investment dries up, and housing supply shrinks rather than expands.

Under a vacancy reset framework, the incentive structure flips. When a tenant vacates, owners can reset the rent to market levels only if they've completed necessary code-compliance work. As Burgos explains in the episode , this dual requirement ensures that both tenant protection and building health move forward together. The incoming tenant then enters the rent-stabilization system with full protections—freezes, moderation clauses, and all existing tenant rights—eliminating concerns that vacancy resets are a backdoor deregulation.

"A vacancy reset does not increase rent on any single in-place tenant today, it doesn't cost the city or state government a dollar, and it brings housing supply on the market, softening free market rents."

The economic argument rests on three pillars. First, building valuations recover , enabling owners to refinance, maintain properties, and invest in capital projects without a government subsidy. Third, by making rent-stabilized buildings investable again, the policy expands the total housing stock discussed in the podcast , which pressures free-market rents downward by increasing overall supply.

Currently, the rent-stabilized sector faces a crisis: over 80% of the 1 million rent-stabilized units are pre-1974 buildings , many of which are aging rapidly. Additionally, approximately 10% of rent-stabilized stock is cash-flow negative, meaning owners lose money on operations each month. Under these conditions, no new rent-stabilized housing is built, and existing stock deteriorates. A vacancy reset is designed to break this cycle without eliminating the core tenant protections that define the system.
Why vacancy reset avoids the traps of other reform proposals

Many rent-stabilization reforms either abandon tenant protection (Costa Hawkins in California) or require perpetual government spending (traditional affordable housing subsidies). A vacancy reset avoids both extremes. The incoming tenant receives the same stabilization umbrella as any other protected tenant—rents can only rise by the percentage set by the Rent Guidelines Board each year, and the unit remains stabilized permanently, subject to succession rights.

The policy also sidesteps the political blockade that has frozen rent reform in New York. Because it does not touch existing tenants and costs the government nothing, it can theoretically appeal to tenant advocates (who gain housing stock) and property owners (who gain investability) simultaneously. questions/beyond-the-plan/what-defines-a: A collaborative working culture exists when people will act in situations without certainty of their commercial outcome to benefit the overall project, and when one party will take actions to their own detriment if it allows the achievement of the collective goal. It is fundamentally about resolving problems beyond individual functional or organisational boundaries.

The distinction here is crucial: collaboration is not simply agreement or cooperation on paper. It emerges when people prioritise the project outcome over their individual interests , even when doing so carries personal cost. This happens not because contracts force it, but because the shared values and behaviours of the team make it possible.

According to Brett Ackroyd in the episode , most project failures do not stem from budgets, timelines, or scope alone—they emerge from fractured relationships and misaligned incentives after the contract is signed. The real work of collaboration begins once the contract is executed, not before.
When Values and Behaviours Align With Systems

People operate because of their values and behaviours , not because of contractual clauses. This insight explains why two projects with identical contracts can deliver vastly different results. If your organisation has clarity around what values and behaviours are non-negotiable, you can examine the surrounding systems and processes to identify gaps or barriers that undermine those values.

This is where frameworks like ISO 44001 become relevant—they provide a structured approach to collaborative working that extends far beyond the contract document itself. Ackroyd discusses how elite delivery teams use such frameworks to embed collaboration as a cultural practice rather than a compliance exercise.

Real-world evidence supports this approach. Projects using collaborative working methods have demonstrated significantly reduced delay times compared to non-collaborative counterparts, as seen in infrastructure projects across Australia and internationally, including Scottish Water's experience.

"You will know a collaborative culture exists when one party will take it on themselves to actually act to their detriment for the other party, because that allows for the achievement of the overall outcome."

Brett Ackroyd — Commercial Lawyer with 25 to 26 years of experience in mega projects within the Department of Defence and Government Security, as well as other industries. He has spent significant time working within major organisations seeking to engage industry on complex project delivery outcomes, with particular focus on moving projects to success after contract execution.

What makes this definition practical is that it is testable. You can observe whether parties genuinely act in cross-boundary problem-solving, or whether they retreat into blame-shifting and contractual posturing when pressure mounts. The episode explores specific methods that defence and government projects use to maintain this culture at scale , even as projects become more complex and involve multiple organisations and stakeholders.
Collaborative culture is defined by action beyond individual interest—people must be willing to absorb cost to serve the collective project outcome.
Contracts are necessary but insufficient; the critical phase for building collaboration is after the contract is signed and execution begins.
Alignment of values and behaviours must be supported by systems and processes that remove barriers to cross-functional and cross-organisational problem-solving.
Projects demonstrating collaborative working practices report measurably reduced delays and improved outcomes compared to siloed delivery models.
questions/beyond-the-plan/how-should-bus: Collaborative working is a systemic approach to managing business relationships that must be intentional, enduring, and scalable. Organisations need to integrate business relationship management into their overall integrated management system, backed by frameworks like ISO 44001, rather than relying solely on personal relationships that become fragile when individuals change roles or project phases shift.

questions/beyond-the-plan/why-does-good-: Good governance is invisible because it works seamlessly —processes flow together, decisions are made, project teams feel supported, and it becomes business as usual. The Visibility Gap: Why Success Goes Unnoticed

When governance functions properly, no one talks about it. Teams receive clear decision-making authority, risk is managed transparently, and stakeholders know who decides what and when. questions/beyond-the-plan/what-is-the-co: Managing under pressure means you are handling your own performance adequately, but leading under pressure means you are actively helping your team navigate difficult phases as well. As a project manager, staying calm and providing clarity and direction to your team remains essential even when facing severe financial, time, personnel, or third-party pressures.

The distinction matters because many project managers conflate coping with crisis with actually leading their team through it. You might be meeting your own deadlines and maintaining your composure, yet if your team is confused, demoralised, or left without clear direction, you're only managing yourself—not leading.

Real leadership under pressure involves communicating with transparency . Your team needs to understand what constraints exist, what options remain on the table, and what you expect from them. Without that clarity, pressure cascades downward as anxiety rather than focus.
"It is not necessarily what the project manager knows that makes the difference. It is how they can work with the team."

questions/beyond-the-plan/how-has-the-ro: The project manager role transformed from a technical position filled by the most senior expert in a field into a leadership role centered on stakeholder engagement and soft skills. From Senior Engineer to People Leader

In the 1950s and 1960s, when the term "project manager" was first coined, the role belonged to the most experienced technical specialist in the room —a senior bridge engineer overseeing bridge construction, or the most skilled person in any given field. These were accidental project managers, people who had climbed so high in their technical expertise that project leadership fell to them naturally.

This model assumed that deep technical knowledge was the foundation of leadership. The project manager's authority came from knowing more about the work than anyone else on the team. Over seven decades, this premise inverted entirely. As Nick Jagger explains in the episode , the discipline shifted to prioritizing expertise in communication, stakeholder engagement, and emotional intelligence over technical depth.
"It is not necessarily what the project manager knows that makes the difference. It is how they can work with the team."

A man-hour is one person working for one hour . If three crew members work one hour on a project, that job consumes three man-hours of labor. The math is straightforward: if your target rate is $100 per man-hour and a job requires three man-hours, your minimum charge is $300.

After finishing a job three or more times, you compare actual hours worked against your budget to see whether you stayed on target, came in under, or exceeded it. If actual hours consistently exceed budgeted hours, you're not hitting your target man-hour rate—meaning you either need to raise prices or improve efficiency.
Why budgeted hours matter: the immediate profitability signal

Tracking budgeted hours versus actual hours is the fastest way to identify which jobs are genuinely profitable . Many lawn care owners bill by the job, not explicitly by the hour, but they're still earning an hourly rate underneath—they just don't always realize it. This invisible hourly wage is where most profitability problems hide.

When a job consistently eats more time than budgeted, you have two concrete problems to solve. You either haven't priced it high enough for the work involved, or your team isn't working efficiently enough . A budgeted hours system shows you which one immediately—without guessing.
The three-job rule: when data becomes actionable

Don't panic over a single job that runs over budget; as Cornell Mack explains in the LCR Media Podcast , you need to complete a job three or more times before the pattern becomes real . One over-run could be bad weather, a miscommunication, or a client change order. Three over-runs is a pricing or efficiency crisis.

This threshold also protects you from over-correcting on fluky jobs. Once you've done the same job repeatedly and see the hours consistently exceed budget, you have legitimate data to act on—not just an outlier.
From data to action: pricing or process

The insight hidden in budgeted hours is whether you should raise your price or tighten your process . A job that takes longer than budgeted could mean your estimate was too optimistic, your crew needs better training, or your equipment isn't efficient enough. Budgeted hours let you distinguish between these scenarios by looking at whether the overrun happens consistently across different crew members or only with one team.

If the overrun appears across all crews, the job itself is underpriced or underestimated. If it's tied to one crew, you have a training or efficiency opportunity. Either way, you now have a data-driven reason to act, discussed at length in this podcast episode on hourly profitability tracking.

questions/lcr-media-podcast/what-ineffic: Four critical inefficiencies drain lawn care profitability: excessive drive time between properties (solved by clustering jobs geographically), poor equipment maintenance causing mid-job breakdowns, employees failing to pre-gather supplies or fuel before starting, and using slow equipment like 21-inch push mowers on larger yards instead of zero-turn or stand-on mowers. Small time losses of five minutes per job—retrieving trimmer string, repairing equipment, walking inefficiently—compound across multiple daily jobs and directly slash your effective hourly earnings.
The compounding cost of small time losses

When you work by the hour in lawn care, every minute directly affects your take-home earnings. A five-minute delay retrieving supplies, waiting for equipment repairs, or walking back for a forgotten tool might seem minor in isolation, but these losses repeat across five, ten, or fifteen jobs per day and accumulate into significant lost income.

As discussed in this episode of the LCR Media Podcast , the difference between struggling business owners and those "crushing it" often comes down to recognizing that profitability is built minute by minute, not project by project.
Four specific inefficiencies to eliminate immediately

Route density is the first major leak. Excessive drive time between geographically scattered properties drains time that produces no revenue. By clustering jobs in the same neighborhood or area, crews spend less time traveling and more time billing. This single change can dramatically improve hourly earnings without raising prices.

Poor equipment maintenance creates unpredictable breakdowns mid-job. A mower that fails halfway through a lawn forces crews to stop, troubleshoot, and repair—turning billable time into dead time. Regular maintenance prevents these costly interruptions and keeps work moving.

Lack of supply preparation means crews start jobs incomplete. If employees don't pre-gather fuel, trimmer string, or other supplies before leaving the shop or arriving at the first property, they'll spend five, ten, or fifteen minutes mid-morning or between jobs retrieving what they forgot. Implementing a simple pre-job checklist prevents this routine drain.

Using undersized equipment on larger yards slows production unnecessarily. A 21-inch push mower takes significantly longer to cut a 10,000-square-foot yard than a zero-turn or stand-on mower. Investing in faster equipment for appropriate job sizes raises your throughput and therefore your hourly rate, as detailed in the full podcast discussion .

questions/lcr-media-podcast/when-should-: Invest in equipment upgrades like zero-turn or stand-on mowers when your current equipment—such as walk-behind mowers—prevents you from hitting your target man-hour rate due to slower speed and operator fatigue. These upgrades allow you to reduce the budgeted hours assigned to each job, directly improving your hourly profitability.
When speed and fatigue become profit limiters

The core decision is straightforward: equipment should pay for itself through efficiency gains. A walk-behind mower requires constant operator input and causes fatigue over long workdays, which slows job completion and forces you to budget more hours per project than faster equipment would require.

Zero-turn mowers deliver three concrete advantages. First, they complete yards faster than walk-behinds due to higher ground speed and tighter turning radius. Second, they reduce operator fatigue, meaning your crew stays productive through full shifts without performance degradation. Third, they eliminate the inefficiency of velcro-style attachments on walk-behinds that require manual setup and adjustments between tasks.
The cash flow reality: save aggressively or lower your rate

Equipment upgrades require capital investment, and timing depends on your current cash position and profitability target. As detailed in this episode on man-hour rate strategy , you have two paths if you cannot afford upgrades immediately.

Path one: start with a lower man-hour rate target that your current equipment can sustain profitably, then aggressively save earnings to fund equipment purchases as quickly as possible. Path two: delay upgrading until you have accumulated sufficient cash flow—but understand that you're sacrificing efficiency and profitability during that period. The faster you upgrade, the sooner you unlock the cost savings and increased job capacity that better equipment provides.

For example, if a walk-behind mower forces you to budget five hours for a job that a zero-turn could complete in three hours, you're leaving profit on the table on every single job until you upgrade. When you factor this across dozens of projects per month, the financial impact compounds quickly.

questions/lcr-media-podcast/how-do-mater: Landscaping projects with materials—flowers, bushes, trees, mulch, or weed control—require pricing that bundles both the material cost (marked up for profit) plus labor calculated at service-specific man-hour rates . Building material costs into the quote

Material costs are straightforward: whatever you pay for mulch, plants, fertilizer, or weed-control products gets marked up and added to the labor total. If a landscape bed job takes three hours with two people, that's three man-hours at $155/hour ($465 in labor) plus materials. Building infrastructure before the crisis hits

The answer to "what would break first?" becomes your roadmap. If it's your team, you know you need to hire or train. If it's your technology, you need infrastructure upgrades. If it's your vendor relationships, you need backup suppliers. Your breaking point is your priority list for the next quarter.

Most business owners stop asking questions far too early. Use the 'five whys' technique—ask why five times in succession —to move past surface symptoms and uncover the actual problem beneath the complaint. Customers rarely identify the real issue themselves; they report what they see, not what causes it.

When you encounter a complaint on Reddit, review sites, or the Better Business Bureau , your first instinct is often to address the immediate grievance. But that's a trap. The complaint you read is the symptom, not the disease.

The five whys method forces you past the obvious. You ask why once—"Why did this customer experience a delay?"—and you get an answer: "The order wasn't processed quickly." Then you ask why again: "Why wasn't the order processed quickly?" Now you learn the real reason might be a system failure, not human error. Keep asking. By the fifth why, you've usually reached the root cause—the thing that, if fixed, prevents the problem from happening again to the next customer.

Too many owners ask why once, declare victory, and implement a surface-level fix . They'll hire faster staff or add a step in the workflow. But if the underlying problem was that your software didn't send notifications properly, hiring won't solve it. The complaint will resurface with the next customer, draining time and resources.

This deeper analysis, as Stuart Webb explains in the episode , applies whether you're monitoring Reddit threads, LinkedIn discussions, or traditional review platforms . The venue doesn't matter; the discipline of drilling down does.

Many networkers collect business cards like trophies, believing that 500 shallow contacts are more useful than 20 deep relationships built on genuine mutual interest. A map of value is fundamentally different: each person in your network has a specific zone of genius, and you understand how that maps onto others.

When you shift to this mindset, networking becomes less about "how do I extract value from this person" and more about "where does this person's strength solve someone else's problem." This is where the AI agent approach becomes powerful —it scales the ability to maintain that map and spot the gaps where one person's struggle is another's superpower.

The practical payoff is immediate: when you approach someone from a position of "I see what you are great at and I can amplify that," the conversation opens instead of closing. Trust builds faster. Introductions flow naturally. And most importantly, people actually remember you and want to stay connected , because you have proven that you see them, not just what they can do for you.
questions/creatures-of-the-industry/what: The Occupational Health and Safety Act, introduced in 1985, gave workers unprecedented legal power to challenge unsafe practices. Terry Riggs, working as a health and safety representative at Shell Refinery, issued 12 pin notices on safety violations—all but one upheld by WorkSafe—forcing the company to implement major changes and make employers face real consequences for the first time.
Workers gained genuine enforcement power

Before 1985, safety violations in Australian heavy industry were largely unpoliced from the ground level. The new act equipped workers themselves with the authority to document breaches and escalate them to the regulator, fundamentally shifting the balance of power on job sites. Riggs, trained through an associate diploma in occupational health and safety at Holmesglen TAFE, became one of the first generation of safety representatives to operate under the new framework.

At the Shell Refinery during a major upgrade project involving a new cracker unit, as described in the episode , Riggs tested the act's teeth. Eleven of his twelve pin notices were upheld by WorkSafe , meaning the regulator agreed with his findings and forced Shell to correct the violations. That compliance rate was staggering in an industry where management had previously operated with minimal oversight.
A major shock to employer culture

Employers in heavy industry had never experienced this kind of scrutiny before. Riggs recalls the moment as "a big slap around the face" for companies that assumed workplace safety was their exclusive domain to manage—or ignore. The act didn't just penalise unsafe conditions; it empowered workers to name them and demand remediation in real time.

Rather than accept defeat, some employers learned a critical lesson. According to the full episode , management subsequently developed "a few paper skills which covered some of the failings of their systems"—meaning they began documenting and formalizing safety procedures to avoid future challenges. The cultural shift was real: companies moved from reactive damage control to proactive system design.
"They got a big slap around the face."

questions/creatures-of-the-industry/how-: WorkCover paid enough to live on, but it couldn't replace the majority of a construction worker's wage—which comes from overtime and other conditions rather than the base hourly rate. Social isolation during years of recovery added a crushing psychological cost that no compensation formula could address.
The Gap Between Base Pay and Real Earnings

The majority of a construction worker's wage isn't his hourly rate —it's his overtime and other conditions. As explained in this episode of Creatures of the Industry , Terry Riggs sustained a scaphoid fracture that kept him out of work for two years. While the compensation covered basic living expenses, it bore no relation to the actual income he lost through missed overtime.

Construction work operates on a different financial structure than most employment. The base rate is merely the foundation; real earning power comes from extended hours, shift premiums, and project-specific allowances. WorkCover assessments, however, typically calculate benefits based on ordinary time earnings—a fundamental mismatch that leaves injured workers financially adrift.
Isolation Beyond the Paycheck

The financial shortfall was only half the story. Two years without work meant two years without the social structure that defines site life . Riggs described the psychological toll plainly: "You haven't got enough money to buy yourself whiskey and you haven't got the usual social interaction and that's a big change."

Construction sites create a peculiar form of community—tight-knit teams working through shared physical demands and workplace hazards. During injury recovery, workers lose both the financial security of that work and the daily human contact that sustains it. WorkCover compensation addressed the first need inadequately, and the second need not at all. This period of isolation, detailed further in the full episode , reveals how workplace injury extends far beyond the physical healing process.
"The majority of a construction worker's wage isn't his hourly rate. It's his overtime and other conditions. That's what I missed."

questions/creatures-of-the-industry/what: The Port Hedland project in the late 1990s had virtually no union representation or organizational structure —no shop committees, no delegate committees, and almost no worker voice despite employing 2,000 people. Workers faced a casualized, de-unionized environment with half a dozen different pay rates , with some receiving cash bonuses collected before leave periods, while scaffolders were among the few who maintained any autonomy within their crews.
A fragmented workforce with no collective voice

On a site of that scale, the absence of formal worker organization was striking. Riggs describes the Port Hedland project as heavily casualized, meaning workers were hired on temporary, short-term contracts with minimal job security. There was no union solidarity whatsoever , even as workers came from all backgrounds—Italian, Greek, Spanish, Irish, English, and Fijian origins all represented on the same job.

The pay structure itself reinforced fragmentation. With workers receiving multiple rates across the workforce , there was no unified wage baseline. Some workers collected cash payments per hour directly before their roster leave—what Riggs describes as informal bonus arrangements rather than transparent contractual conditions. This system made it nearly impossible for workers to organize collectively around pay and conditions, as no two workers necessarily shared the same deal.

As discussed in detail in this episode of Creatures of the Industry , the roster itself created additional isolation: workers operated on a seven-weeks-on, one-week-off cycle, rotating through remote Western Australia's Northwest Shelf region. This pattern limited face-to-face organizing time and reinforced geographic distance from union support networks.
Scaffolders: the only exception to powerlessness

While most trades had no meaningful representation, scaffolders maintained some operational autonomy within their crews —a small but significant difference. This wasn't formal union power; it was practical craft control. Scaffolders could exercise judgment about how work was done within their gangs, though even this was constrained by the broader casualized structure of the site.

Riggs, working as a rigger with decades of health and safety experience, found himself operating without institutional backing. The 1985 Occupational Health and Safety Act had equipped workers like him with legal rights to raise safety issues, yet the Port Hedland site's lack of delegate structures meant individual safety representatives worked largely in isolation , unable to mobilize collective enforcement.

questions/creatures-of-the-industry/how-: After the explosion that killed five people, the remediation and reconstruction of the Longford Gas Plant became one of the most substantial construction jobs available to workers in the region . The state government invested heavily in the project, providing workers with improved conditions: 12-hour shifts, on-site accommodation at 90 Mile Beach, a dedicated canteen, and shuttle bus access across the massive facility.
Remediation work as rare opportunity

Terry Riggs secured work with Fleur Daniel on the remediation and construction phases that followed the 1998 disaster. He describes this as one of only half a dozen truly good jobs throughout his entire career in construction. The scale of the project was significant enough to absorb substantial numbers of skilled workers across multiple trades.

Though the state government's flooding of resources created the opportunity, it also came with trade-offs. Workers faced long 12-hour shifts punctuated by periods of little work , a pattern typical of large-scale industrial remediation where mobilization and demobilization cycles left gaps in productivity.
Infrastructure for the workforce

What distinguished this job from many others was the employer's provision of comprehensive support systems. Workers received accommodation directly on the 90 Mile Beach site , removing the burden of finding housing in the surrounding area. A canteen operated on-site, and a dedicated shuttle bus system transported workers across the sprawling facility.

As Riggs explains in Creatures of the Industry , the broader contrast between this project and others he worked on—particularly the casualized, de-unionized conditions on other major industrial projects—illustrates how state investment could temporarily reshape working standards. The Longford remediation represented a relatively protected employment environment, even if the work itself remained physically demanding.

questions/creatures-of-the-industry/what: Major oil and gas companies like Woodside and Esso maintain extensive documentation claiming "world's best safety practice" that remains unused and unopened in filing folders. When incidents occur, these companies conduct investigations that target the least powerful workers as scapegoats while the safety documentation never leaves the shelf—a systemic failure to implement the safety systems they publicly promote.

This contradiction sits at the heart of corporate safety culture in heavy industry. According to Terry Riggs, a scaffolder and health and safety representative with decades of experience across major Australian industrial projects, the gap between documented safety protocols and actual workplace practice creates a dangerous two-tier accountability system.
Documentation as a liability shield, not a safety tool

The real purpose of these safety folders, as described in the episode , appears to be legal protection rather than worker protection. Companies can point to their comprehensive safety documentation in court or regulatory proceedings, even as workers on the ground operate without access to or awareness of these protocols.

When incidents trigger "root and branch investigations," the focus shifts away from systemic failures in safety management and toward individual workers—typically those with the least power to defend themselves. Riggs witnessed junior workers subjected to intensive scrutiny, questioned for weeks, and ultimately dismissed, while the safety systems themselves escaped examination.

The irony is stark: the same documentation that companies tout as evidence of their commitment to "world-class safety" becomes invisible the moment a worker is injured or killed. It sits on shelves, as Riggs puts it bluntly, and "never come off the fucking shelf." This reveals a structural failure where safety management is decoupled from actual safety practice—a gap that transfers risk from the company's systems to the individual worker.

Union membership has shifted from a foundation of shared values and workplace comradeship to a purely transactional relationship driven by money and hourly rates . On major projects like the Metro Tunnel, workers no longer experience the meaningful interaction with colleagues that once defined construction culture. As Riggs observes, "the brothers have just had it too good for too long and they've lost perspective"—union solidarity no longer binds workers through adversity, but rather fragments them into individual wage-seekers.
From comradeship to cash transactions

The transformation reflects a fundamental rupture in how construction workers relate to their labour and to each other. Where earlier generations understood union membership as a collective commitment rooted in shared struggle and mutual protection , current workers treat it as a contractual arrangement focused on extracting maximum hourly compensation.

This shift extends beyond attitude to material working conditions. As Terry Riggs explains in the podcast , the majority of a construction worker's wage is not the hourly rate itself but the overtime and conditions stacked on top—a reality that has reshaped how workers calculate value and view their union membership.
Loss of adversity as social glue

Earlier periods of construction work were marked by hazardous conditions that forged genuine workplace bonds. Meaningful interaction with workmates through shared hardship created the foundation of construction culture . These bonds were not sentimental—they were survival mechanisms born from industry-wide dangers, from the scaffolding heights to the refinery heat.

The contemporary construction worker, particularly on high-profile projects like the Metro Tunnel, no longer experiences this crucible. Without that shared adversity, the social fabric that once held workers together has unravelled. The result is what Riggs terms the absence of "solidarity and no comradeship"—a workplace stripped of the collective identity that once transcended individual wages.
"The brothers have just had it too good for too long and they've lost perspective."

In the 1970s, scaffolders obtained a permit valid for 12 months to 2 years , during which they documented their on-the-job experience before attending formal instruction at a technical college. The real education came from learning alongside experienced scaffolders who taught the custom and practice of the trade—knowledge more powerful than any written regulation when few rules existed.

The pathway combined practical apprenticeship with institutional learning. After working on site for the duration of their permit period, apprentice scaffolders enrolled in classes at technical institutes like Swinburne. As Terry Riggs describes in the episode , the instructors themselves were former practitioners—his own instructor at Swinburne, Mr Roberts, was the chief scaffold inspector, bringing real-world authority to the classroom.
The dominance of on-the-job training over written rules

What made this training system distinctive was the primacy of experience over documentation. When Riggs transitioned to scaffolding in the early 1980s after ten years as a labourer, custom and practice—the unwritten knowledge held by veteran scaffolders—held more weight than any formal regulation . The building and construction industry had few written safety codes; the trade was governed by established methods passed directly from master to apprentice.

Riggs himself endured the full rigour of this dual commitment: after an 11-hour workday on site, he would ride his motorcycle for over an hour to attend evening or after-hours classes at the technical institute. This grueling schedule reflected how seriously both employer and worker treated formal qualification, yet it remained secondary to the daily mentoring that occurred on the scaffolding itself. The full episode explores how these informal apprenticeships shaped an entire generation of Australian construction professionals.

In the era before scaffolding work was heavily regulated, the construction site itself became a school. As described in Creatures of the Industry , the relationship between experienced and apprentice scaffolders was built on observation, correction, and earned trust—not compliance with written procedures.
The lead hand as safety keeper

The most critical figure in this informal system was the lead hand, whose watchfulness kept younger workers alive . This person held authority not through a title but through demonstrated competence and years of working safely on complex projects. They knew every hazard before it became dangerous.

A lead hand would train newcomers by placing them in progressively more challenging positions—never throwing an untested worker into work at height until they had proven themselves capable. This gradual exposure ensured that by the time someone was working 70 metres in the air, they had internalized the rhythms and risks of the job through months of supervised practice.
Belonging to a gang meant knowing the code

Custom and practice was also about integration into a work community with unwritten but absolute standards . A scaffolder didn't just learn techniques; they learned what it meant to be part of a gang. This sense of belonging created accountability—letting down the gang or breaking an unspoken rule carried social weight that often exceeded any formal penalty.

questions/creatures-of-the-industry/what: Most scaffolders wore out their knees or backs from carrying heavy, concentrated loads, typically on one shoulder without alternating. A right-handed scaffolder would carry the load on the right shoulder, putting a big load on the right knee, which eventually failed for most people — the cumulative vertical strain from knees to hips to shoulders meant something in the system would inevitably fail.

The occupational health crisis among scaffolders was rooted in a simple structural reality: 95% of scaffolding work involves carrying tons of steel to or away from the job site . Unlike machinery or tools that distribute load evenly, steel beams and scaffold components are rigid, heavy objects that demand one-sided body positioning across an entire working career.

This wasn't a matter of poor technique or weak workers. Experienced scaffolders like Terry Riggs, who worked on major projects including offshore construction at Barry Beach from 1978 to 1983 , faced the same inevitable wear. The problem was systemic to the work itself—no amount of skill or care could prevent the toll of sustained asymmetrical loading on a single side of the body.
Why the right shoulder and knee failed first

For right-handed workers, the pattern was predictable. Picking up a scaffold tube or steel beam naturally fell to the dominant side, making the right shoulder the primary load bearer. This created a cascade of failure: the concentrated weight stressed the right knee, which bore the gravitational and stabilizing load unevenly , then radiating upward through the hip, spine, and shoulders.

The body's interconnected skeletal system meant that compensating for knee pain shifted strain to the lower back and hips. A worker might favour their left leg to ease right knee pressure, only to develop chronic back or hip issues. The cumulative injury pattern was almost universal among long-term scaffolders, as detailed in the full Creatures of the Industry episode .
The lack of rotation and recovery

Scaffolding work offered almost no mechanism for load alternation. Unlike jobs where workers might rotate between different tasks or switch shoulders mid-day, scaffolding demanded continuous, repetitive carrying of heavy objects in the same body position. There was no built-in recovery time for asymmetrical strain to dissipate .

This relentless, single-sided loading distinguished scaffolding from other physically demanding trades. A concrete worker or bricklayer might vary their movements and body positions throughout the day. A scaffolder, by contrast, executed the same shoulder-load motion thousands of times across decades, with minimal deviation. The interview reveals how Riggs and his peers simply accepted this as the cost of the trade —a silent occupational sacrifice that nobody talked about until bodies failed.

Boom lifts introduced a critical construction flaw: not all fittings were properly completed during assembly. When a scaffold was built using a boom lift rather than conventional hanging methods, the transom fitting could go unfinished while the ledger fitting was secured , leaving tubes vulnerable to collapse.

Terry Riggs witnessed this danger firsthand in Port Hedland around 1998. At a 70-metre tower, a tube dropped because while the ledger fitting had been tightened, the transom fitting remained incomplete. The tube fell with terrifying speed—saved from catastrophe only by a vessel's protrusion that broke its fall. Without that chance obstruction, Riggs and his off-sider would have come off the scaffold entirely.

This wasn't an isolated mishap. The shift from conventional hanging scaffold methods to boom lift assembly fundamentally changed how work was sequenced on site. In hanging scaffold construction, workers had time and physical access to verify every fitting was properly torqued before moving to the next stage. Boom lifts accelerated the process but introduced gaps in the workflow where supervisors might assume fittings were complete without verification.

As discussed at length in this podcast episode , the real danger lay in the assumption. A ledger fitting done up could mask an incomplete transom fitting on the opposite side of the joint, creating an asymmetric load condition that destabilized the entire vertical support.

The deeper issue revealed in Riggs' account is that boom lift convenience removed the built-in verification steps that older methods enforced. In traditional hanging scaffold work, the physical labour of manual assembly meant multiple workers had to touch and check each joint. Boom lifts compressed that labour—and accidentally compressed the safety checks along with it.
Incomplete fittings created asymmetric load failure

The fittings on a scaffold joint work in pairs: the ledger connects the scaffold frame horizontally to the building or structure, and the transom supports the platform perpendicular to it. A completed ledger with an incomplete transom creates a one-sided anchor point , making the structure vulnerable to twisting and pulling forces it wasn't designed to resist.

At 70 metres, even a partially supported tube becomes a falling object with fatal kinetic energy. The margin for error at that height is zero. What makes this failure mode particularly dangerous is its invisibility—a worker standing on the platform might see a fitting that looks secured without any way to verify the joint on the far side is also torqued. The boom lift method removed the redundant human verification that custom and practice had built into the older system.

When scaffold standards are not staggered and all joins align on a single level, the entire structure can collapse catastrophically , with standards pulling out of their connections and the scaffold hanging into the street or surrounding area.

This structural principle lies at the heart of scaffold safety, yet it represents one of the most dangerous oversights in construction. Terry Riggs witnessed this failure firsthand during his decades of work across Australian building sites.
A Real Collapse: Russell Street, 1980s

During the 1980s, Terry Riggs observed a scaffolding disaster on Russell Street that exemplified this structural weakness. The scaffold had been erected without proper staggering of the standard joints—meaning every vertical post connection aligned at the same height.

The result was immediate and catastrophic: the standards pulled out of their spigots on the building side , causing the entire scaffolding to hang loose into Russell Street below. This wasn't a minor failure or a minor slump. This was a complete structural breach that exposed workers and the public to severe danger.

Such incidents reveal more than just an engineering mistake. They signal, as discussed in the episode , a loss of the skill and knowledge that had previously governed how scaffolds were properly erected—knowledge passed through hands-on experience and custom practice among experienced scaffolders.

These gatherings functioned as peer-to-peer learning forums where custom and practice were debated and refined by rank-and-file workers, not imposed from above.
The meetings reinforced a cultural standard: technical skill was inseparable from interpersonal cooperation and willingness to be held accountable by fellow workers.
questions/creatures-of-the-industry/how-: No, changing administrations won't shift industry culture on its own. Government overreach causes far more harm to workers than administrative shifts —Ray Smith compares the current era to the ABCC period, where construction workers had fewer rights than convicted murderers and rapists.

Ray Smith's perspective challenges the notion that simply rotating leadership or adjusting regulatory frameworks will meaningfully protect workers or reshape how the industry operates. The real damage, he argues, comes from government bodies that prioritize monuments to their own legacy over accountability for the conditions workers face on site.

Government agencies, Smith contends, pursue agendas that benefit the state rather than the workforce. They seek visible projects to justify their tenure but accept no responsibility for workplace deaths, injuries, or exploitation that occurs during execution. This structural indifference places the burden of member protection entirely on unions themselves.

Ray Smith — Construction Worker, Delegate, and Tour Manager. After spending nearly 30 years in the music industry from the mid-1970s to the mid-1990s—working as a roadie and tour manager for acts including Cold Chisel, the Rolling Stones, Joe Cocker, and Oasis—Smith transitioned to construction. He became a delegate representing union members across mixed metals, civil engineering, building, and infrastructure projects in Melbourne and regional Victoria, gaining decades of direct experience navigating union-management relations and regulatory frameworks.

In the episode, Smith explores the specific parallels between the ABCC era and modern regulatory overreach , drawing on his lived experience as both a worker and a union representative. His argument rests on a simple premise: **unions must be the primary safeguard for members** because governments will never take genuine responsibility for worker safety or dignity.

The implication is stark. Industry culture shifts only when union power remains strong and vigilant—not when governments change personnel or issue new policies. Protecting workers requires constant defense against both negligent employers and government bodies that view construction sites as mere backdrops for political achievement rather than spaces where human lives are at stake.
questions/creatures-of-the-industry/what: The construction union will remain indispensable as long as workers exist —Ray Smith firmly rejects any notion that deregulation could undermine its necessity. Unions deal with fatalities, injuries, and worker exploitation while facing undeserved criticism; the solution is not to dismantle them, but to recognize their vital protective function.

Ray Smith's conviction rests on a straightforward principle: workers will always require collective representation . In his view, the union's future is secure not because of regulatory mandates, but because the fundamental challenges it addresses—safety violations, wage theft, workplace injuries—remain endemic to the industry. As long as these problems persist, the organization that fights them will remain necessary.

The frustration Smith expresses is revealing. Unions handle the difficult work of confronting fatalities, injuries, and systematic rip-offs while being blamed for perceived rigidity or obstruction. This inversion of responsibility—where the problem-solver faces criticism instead of the problem itself—points to a deeper misunderstanding of the union's role in the sector, as discussed in detail in this episode of Creatures of the Industry .
"For as long as there are people doing what they do, there's most certainly a role for the unions to play."

Ray Smith — Construction Worker, Delegate, and Tour Manager. The trajectory he envisions is one in which unions evolve in response to changing industry conditions, but never become obsolete because the need for worker protection does not become obsolete.

Understanding this long-term trajectory requires recognizing that union strength is rooted in material reality —the concrete need for collective defense against exploitation—rather than bureaucratic privilege. Any serious challenge to union influence would need to address the underlying problems unions solve, not simply attempt to remove the organizations that solve them. Learn more about Ray Smith's full perspective on industry culture and regulatory change in the full episode .

Ray Smith left school around 1975–1976 and spent nearly 30 years in the music industry as a roadie and manager , working with acts including Johnny Diesel and the Injectors—the first Australian band to sell half a million copies. He eventually stepped away from the touring circuit and moved into construction, where he discovered a deeper sense of belonging through the camaraderie and union representation work that followed.
From Roadie to Tour Manager

Ray's entry into the music world was deeply personal. His father played drums and was active in bands, inspiring young Ray to pursue a career in the industry rather than a conventional path. He began as a roadie carrying equipment at venues, earning modest wages—around five to ten dollars per night during the 1970s and 80s—while working five to seven nights a week. Over time, he developed the skills and relationships that elevated him to tour management.

His management portfolio became impressive: Ray worked with Johnny Diesel and the Injectors during their rise to national prominence, and also handled touring logistics for major international acts including Cold Chisel, the Rolling Stones, Joe Cocker, and Oasis. The details of managing these high-profile tours are explored further in the episode , offering insights into the demands of the touring lifestyle in that era.
The Move to Construction

Ray's transition to construction was not a sudden break but a deliberate step away from the touring circuit. When he first entered the industry, he thought it would be a temporary 12-month engagement —a way to try something new before returning to music management. That plan changed.

The construction sector offered him something the music industry hadn't: genuine human connection and the opportunity to support workers directly. As his role evolved into union delegate work, representing members and advocating for their interests, Ray discovered a sense of purpose that extended beyond logistics and management. His perspective on why construction ultimately felt more fulfilling is detailed in the full conversation , where he reflects on nearly three decades of experience across the entire spectrum of construction work—from mixed metals and civil engineering to infrastructure projects across Melbourne and regional Victoria.
"The fond memories are just the mateship within construction for sure, mate. The characters I've met along the way—that's the highlight definitely."

Ray Smith — Construction Worker and Delegate. Ray Smith began his music industry career around 1975-1976 as a roadie, carrying equipment and building experience with bands like Johnny Diesel and the Injectors, Cold Chisel, and Georgia Satellites. Over nearly 30 years in the touring circuit , he progressed from roadie to manager and eventually tour manager, handling logistics and artist relations for some of the biggest names in international rock and pop. This long tenure gave him deep insight into the realities of high-profile touring.

His work with major acts like the Rolling Stones and Joe Cocker demonstrated his ability to manage complex touring operations at the highest level. As Smith explains in the podcast , the personal relationships that formed during this time—particularly his friendship with Joe Cocker—were as significant as the professional achievements. Cocker trusted Smith enough to ring him directly whenever his tours came to Australia.
Managing the Gallagher brothers and the cost of constant travel

When Oasis came to Australia for their early tour, Smith took on the role of Australian tour manager. One Gallagher brother proved particularly disruptive at Sydney Entertainment Centre , requiring Smith to navigate the tensions and unpredictability that can arise when managing high-ego artists on the road. These moments tested his management skills under real pressure.

Despite the prestige and experience, the relentless cycle of airports, tour buses, planes, trains, and constant movement took a toll that Smith struggled to recover from. What had once seemed like an adventure became exhausting—the human cost of perpetual travel, even with the biggest acts in the world, eventually became unsustainable. As a point detailed in this episode , this realisation led Smith to leave touring entirely and pursue a different path in the construction industry, where he would spend the next chapter of his career.
"The fond memories are just the mateship within construction for sure, mate. The characters I've met along the way—that's the highlight definitely."

questions/creatures-of-the-industry/what: Ray Smith pulled a Gallagher brother from Oasis into a private room during their Sydney Entertainment Centre tour and calmly laid out expectations: respect is non-negotiable when working together . He made it clear that disrespectful behavior wouldn't be tolerated, and the next day, the artist apologized. The artist's London management later thanked Smith for being the first person to establish that boundary.

What made Smith's approach effective wasn't aggression—it was directness combined with professionalism. He didn't shame the artist publicly or escalate the situation. Instead, he removed him from the immediate environment and communicated a simple truth: mutual respect is the foundation of any working relationship.

This moment reveals a principle that Smith had clearly learned during nearly 30 years managing touring musicians —confrontation works best when it's grounded in respect for the other person, even when you're correcting them. Smith treated the artist as someone capable of change, not someone to be written off.

The apology the next day wasn't forced or defensive. It came from genuine recognition that the artist had crossed a line. In touring, where weeks on the road can amplify tension and ego, having a tour manager willing to reset standards is rare. Smith's willingness to have that difficult conversation, rather than letting bad behavior slide, ultimately strengthened the working relationship.

Ray Smith — Tour Manager and Construction Delegate. This suggests the behavior was a known pattern—but no one in the artist's circle had been willing or able to address it until Smith stepped in.

This is where experience matters. Smith had already managed the Rolling Stones and Joe Cocker—acts at the absolute top of the industry. He knew what professionalism looked like at scale. He also knew that one moment of directness, delivered with respect, could reset an entire working relationship.
